Email: matthew.nowlin@uta.edu]" reference-doc: custom-reference-doc.docx --- # Robustness Check: Controlling for Demographics The main text models the effect of cue condition, party identification, and their interaction on energy-source prioritization and willingness-to-pay (WTP) without any additional controls. This appendix reports two robustness checks. This section re-estimates every main-text model controlling for age, male, white, education, and income, and the following section adds concern about the cost of electricity to those demographic controls. As shown below, the coefficients and the substantive conclusions are consistent with the main text, though a few interactions near the .05 threshold move slightly across it. As in the main text, the Trump cue × Republican interaction for any positive WTP was marginally significant (b = 0.65, *p* = .051). For renewables, Democrats were willing to pay \$3.70 more on average, and Republicans \$6.00 less (*p* = .001). The climate cue × Democrat interaction was significant (b = 5.23, *p* = .037), and the climate cue × Republican interaction was similar in size (b = 4.25, *p* = .105), which is the same pattern, with nearly the same magnitudes, reported in the main text without these controls. **Summary.** Adding demographic controls does not change the sign of any cue × party identification coefficient and shifts coefficient magnitudes only slightly. The Trump cue × Republican interaction for the priority scale remains significant (b = -0.53, *p* = .037), and the climate cue × Democrat interaction for the priority scale remains near zero. The main text's cue and party identification effects on energy prioritization and WTP are likely not an artifact of the demographic composition of respondents in each cue and party group. \newpage # Robustness Check: Controlling for Demographics and Concern about Energy Cost Energy affordability was a salient concern during the period of data collection, as respondents' mean concern about the cost of electricity was 7.88 on a 0 to 10 scale. Because this concern could plausibly confound cue and party identification effects on prioritization and WTP, this section re-estimates every main-text model controlling for demographics (age, male, white, education, and income) plus concern about energy cost. As shown below, the coefficients and the substantive conclusions are consistent with the main text. The results for the energy source-priority scale are shown in @tbl-priority-ols-supp, parallel to the priority-scale table in the main text. ::: {#tbl-priority-ols-supp .cell tbl-cap='Effect of cue condition, party identification, and their interaction on the energy source-priority scale, controlling for concern about energy cost (survey-weighted OLS; baseline condition and those who identify with neither party as reference)'} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: For fossil fuels, concern about energy cost was associated with lower odds of any positive WTP among those who identify with neither party, though this effect was only marginally significant (b = -0.12, log-odds scale, *p* = .054), and it did not differ significantly for Democrats (b = 0.08, *p* = .195) or Republicans (b = 0.07, *p* = .314). Among those with any positive fossil-fuel WTP, concern about energy cost lowered the amount they were willing to pay (b = -1.50, *p* = .009), and this penalty was significantly offset under the Trump cue (b = 1.13, *p* = .033). For renewables, concern about energy cost lowered WTP among those who identify with neither party (b = -1.25, *p* = .007), and this penalty was marginally smaller for both Democrats (b = 0.84, *p* = .084) and Republicans (b = 0.82, *p* = .098). The concern-about-cost terms significant at *p* $\leq$ .10 in each model are: **Fossil fuels, any positive WTP (logit):** - Concern about energy cost: b = -0.12, *p* = .054 **Fossil fuels, amount if WTP > \$0 (OLS):** - Concern about energy cost: b = -1.50, *p* = .009 - Trump cue × Concern about energy cost: b = 1.13, *p* = .033 **Renewables, amount (OLS):** - Concern about energy cost: b = -1.25, *p* = .007 - Concern about energy cost × Democrat: b = 0.84, *p* = .084 - Concern about energy cost × Republican: b = 0.82, *p* = .098 **Summary.** Concern about energy cost is not simply a nuisance control, as it is associated with lower WTP for both fossil fuels and renewables, and its dampening effect on the fossil-fuel WTP amount is significantly offset under the Trump cue. Its relationship with energy priority and WTP does not differ significantly by party identification, though for renewables the cost penalty is marginally smaller among partisans than among those who identify with neither party. None of this changes the sign of the main-text cue × party identification effects (@tbl-priority-ols-supp and @tbl-wtp-models-supp), which have similar magnitudes in this specification. \newpage # Covariate Balance across Conditions @tbl-balance shows the unweighted mean of each demographic variable, concern about the cost of electricity, and the two party identification measures in each condition, along with the *p*-value from a one-way F-test of each variable on condition. The conditions differ somewhat in age and in the share of white respondents, which is why the main-text models are also estimated with demographic controls. Party identification was measured after the outcome questions, so the party identification rows also test whether the cues changed how respondents identified. The distribution of party identification did not differ across conditions ($\chi^2$ = 3.29, *df* = 4, *p* = .511). ::: {#tbl-balance .cell tbl-cap='Unweighted means by condition and p-values from one-way F-tests of each variable on condition (party identification was asked after the outcome questions)'} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Variable | Baseline| Trump cue| Climate cue|p | |:-------------------------------------|--------:|---------:|-----------:|:-----| |Age | 42.63| 43.76| 44.51|0.019 | |Male | 0.49| 0.48| 0.49|0.915 | |White | 0.69| 0.70| 0.63|0.002 | |College degree | 0.56| 0.56| 0.55|0.772 | |Income (1-11) | 4.71| 4.55| 4.61|0.415 | |Concern about electricity cost (0-10) | 7.73| 7.81| 7.87|0.326 | |Democrat (post-treatment) | 0.55| 0.58| 0.56|0.208 | |Republican (post-treatment) | 0.29| 0.27| 0.29|0.488 | ::: ::: \newpage # Average Effects of the Cues In the main-text models, the cues are interacted with party identification, so the coefficients for the Trump and climate cues are the effects of the cues among those who identify with neither party only. @tbl-cue-only reports models with the cues alone, which estimate the average effect of each cue across the full sample. The MDE is the smallest interaction effect the design could detect with 80 percent power at a two-sided $\alpha$ = .05, calculated as (1.96 + 0.84) times the standard error. The MDEs for the WTP models are large relative to the estimated interactions, so small effects of the cues on WTP cannot be ruled out. ::: {#tbl-interaction-tests .cell tbl-cap='Cue × party identification interaction terms from the main-text models, with minimum detectable effects (MDE; 80% power, two-sided alpha = .05). Because the models fully interact the cues with party identification, and the party-only weights give every respondent within a party the same weight, the party-only estimates are the same as the unweighted estimates. The demographic-only estimates are close to the estimates with the full weights. As such, the differences between the weighted and unweighted models reflect the demographic weights rather than the party weights.
